newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican gov't may privatize satellite system.
newsitem.headline: Mexican gov't may privatize satellite system.

text.p: Mexico is measuring private interest in owning and operating the nation's current and future satellite systems, government officials said Tuesday.

"We are first trying to determine the level of interest in our various satellite areas. Much depends on what investors say in this first signal of intent," Enrique Cervantes, planning director of Telecommunicaciones de Mexico (Telecomm), told Reuters.
Telecomm is the state-owned agency that operates Mexico's three satellites, its ground satellite infrastructure and the telegraph services.
The government uses the satellite system for military communications, but also rents capacity to the private sector for commercial, educational and entertainment purposes.

The future ownership of Mexico's satellite service depends on what private companies indicate to the government in official proposals that will be accepted starting this week through December 20, the Communications and Transport ministry said in a statement. Cervantes said the government will decide whether to issue stock in the system as a public company or sell it to a single buyer, based on whether investors would like to own or be associates in operating the satellites.

At stake are the three satellites currently in orbit, plus space for four fixed satellites, related ground infrastructure and any future satellites. Mexico has applied for four more fixed satellite orbit positions with the United Nations International Telecommunication Union, Cervantes said.
Net revenue from the three orbiting satellites totals about $120 million a year, but the government has not yet determined the net worth of the entire satellite system, he said.
"Capacity has been rising, but there is a strong potential for further growth," Cervantes said.
The government has already heard from "a significant number" of interested companies, he said.

As with other Mexican privatization schemes, 51 percent of the satellite system would be sold to national companies, with the remainder available to foreign buyers. Both individuals and corporations can apply to operate or own the systems.
"Basically with the speed of changes in technology, (the government) realized the satellites should be in private hands," Cervantes said.
Mexico hopes to decide how it will auction rights to its satellites and begin accepting concrete offers by the third quarter of 1997, Cervantes said.
